utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. Case IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon to everyone on this Wednesday. We'll finish -- or we'll continue with the cross- examination and the end of the cross-examination of Mr. Beese. In line with what my colleagues said yesterday, I'd like to remind you that we are very careful in monitoring the time used by the Defence. We've been able to see that some abuse has been going on in time -- in the use of time, and we might even consider taking sanctions if we find that our directions, our orders, are not complied with. As a result, for the time left for the examination of Mr. Beese, we have one hour and a half until the first break, and then you'll have another hour and a half until the second break, and that will be the end of it. In other words, after the second break, we'll start examining the next witness. Therefore, as a whole for the Defence, and I'm not going to say what time is going to be allocated to the Defence of Mr. Praljak and the previous counsel, on the whole you have three hours left. Let's not waste any more time. I'll now give the floor to the following counsel: The counsel started -- was cross-examining Mr. Beese yesterday. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Yesterday, we asked for two hours. I need to say this for the record: In view of what Your Honour has just said, according to yesterday's decision, I should take an hour and five minutes, but because I don't want to harm the defence of Mr. Praljak, I will do my best within an hour.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Beese, the last document I showed you yesterday was document 2D 00021. It was a Defence order, and I will ask for it to be shown on e-court. I told you yesterday that it was very important, and your response was that you hadn't seen it. I will, however, draw your attention to some portions of this document because I feel it is indeed important. 2D 00021.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, we don't have anything on our screens. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: If we could take a look at point 1.2. That's the lower part -- well, on the next page, in fact. Yes. 1.2. I wish to read the sentence before the last which reads as follows, and you can follow it on the monitor. And let me remind you it's a Defence order: "In subsequent operations, attack from the wing along the following axes: Semovac-Podhum, Balinovac and Centre 2-Rudnik. Assign the seizing of Hum hill to part of the forces." Can we now look at 1.8, and in the translation it's on page 0098. Yes. Thank you. And here it says "The RBH MUP has the task to take positions and defend the old bridge and the newly-built bridge at Musala, and with part of the forces attack the premises of the MUP and the HZ and the Mostar police station." In 1.9, it says: "The reconnaissance platoon has the task of taking the premises of Electrohercegvina. After taking the premises, persistently defend them, and cut-off electricity only when requested from the brigade." From the text of this defence order and the codes we saw yesterday, we may conclude -- well, it's my conclusion that this is an order for attack, in fact. Yesterday, from the report of your mission, 1981 of the 20th of March, we saw that at that time Mr. Ganic was in Mostar. Am I right in saying that? This was the day when, in the report we saw yesterday, it said a meeting had started on the 18th of April and was interrupted by Mr. Stojic. Is that correct? Do you know, yesterday we saw that Mr. Ganic was a member of the Presidency? Are you aware that at the same time he was the Supreme Commander of the armed forces, and do you know that the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina was the Supreme Commander of the army of Bosnia- Herzegovina? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Well, yesterday, you put forward the assumption that Mr. Ganic was the deputy president of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Does not it seem a little illogical that on a day when he's going to Geneva for peace negotiations an order such as this is issued, on the very same day when he is in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is. I'd be very interested to know when this order came into the possession of the HVO headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Well, I think it's much more important to see when it was actually written, but you say you knew nothing about it. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which means it wasn't presented to us by any party, that issuing it or that receiving it, by whatever means.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: At the time we are talking about, and yesterday we concluded that Mr. Stojic intervened that day on the meeting of the 18th of April because of certain attacks and preparations for attack on the HVO. Did you perhaps check whether there were, in fact, any such orders to attack and any attacks?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had no means, nor did my mission, of interrogating the military intentions of either party, but either party was at liberty to present their findings to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes, but from your reports, it follows that the opinions presented to you by the HVO were disregarded by you because you thought it was their propaganda. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was essential that if people came with claims we could substantiate them, that is all.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I will go back to this interrupted meeting. Mr. Stojic said that attacks had been launched on the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The meeting was interrupted in order to check these allegations. Were these allegations, in fact, checked by your mission?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The people to whom Mr. Stojic made these remarks were the head of the ECMM mission in the region, Mr. Prlic and Mr. Ganic. Three very senior people were present to be able to hear the complaint and to react to it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: But my question was different. In view of the fact that the head of your mission was at the meeting, were you given any instructions to check -- within the scope of your mission, to check what Mr. Stojic had said?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was very difficult at that time. There was active conflict under way. We would not have had the resources to check everything we would have wished to do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. I will now move on briefly to another topic. During the examination-in-chief and also during cross- examination, you referred quite often to the situation in Gornji Vakuf in early and mid-January, 1993. Could we please take a look at some documents concerning this topic. Could we see 2D 00093, please. As we can see -- could we look at the date. Yes, the 27th of January, 1993. Mr. Alija Izetbegovic and Mr. Mate Boban signed a joint statement in Geneva, and point 1 is very important to us. "We command that confrontations (clashes) between the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the HVO stop immediately. We call upon the Croatian and Muslim people for complete support because clashes are of use to the aggressor only." Do you remember having seen this statement? Because all this was taking place at the time we are talking about and Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware of the statement. I can't recall, I'm afraid, in what form I saw or heard it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very well. And in connection with this statement, could we look at document 2D 00048. Can we please look at page 001 in order to see what this document is about. And while we're waiting for that page to turn up, it is a document confirming that Mr. Sefer Halilovic, the commander of the armed forces at that time, made a statement for El Pais, a Spanish newspaper. This is his statement. We can show how we obtained this interview if necessary, but I only wish to draw your attention to the date here, the 27th of January, 1993. And I wish to draw attention to the second sentence: "No one can destroy the idea of Bosnia and Herzegovina as a unitary and sovereign state through any kind of negotiating. Negotiations are welcome, but in the opposite case we shall win on the battlefield." This statement was made at the same time when Mr. Boban and Mr. Izetbegovic were signing the joint statement, and here we see unitary Bosnia-Herzegovina. This would be a Bosnia-Herzegovina in which the idea of one man, one vote would prevail, and this was the idea advocated by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the political structures of Bosnia- Herzegovina. Now, look at the next sentence: "Halilovic's opinion most probably has a greater importance even than the opinion of the president, Alija Izetbegovic, since although he does not have a chair negotiating table in Geneva, he represents all those who are fighting on the front lines." I'll show you two more sentences. Could we scroll down a little bit. A little bit more, please. Yes. Now we have it. It's the end of the last paragraph that can be seen on the screen. "In Gornji Vakuf, they learnt a lesson and now they're asking for a cease-fire." Because you said that it was the HVO obstructing negotiations on a cease-fire. Doesn't it follow from this that it was in fact the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina dictating the conditions for a cease-fire and for negotiations? Let's not forget that this is an interview given by Sefer Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I can't comment on the activity in Sarajevo or Geneva at this time, but certainly at the talks around the table in Gornji Vakuf, the instructions given by senior commanders of both sides for a cease-fire and withdrawal were adhered too more readily by one side than the other.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which party adhered to the cease-fire better than the others?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Bosnian Muslim party at the table were more enthusiastic and prepared to withdraw or effect a cease-fire sooner, faster than the HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The counsel read out excerpts of an interview given by Halilovic to El Pais. He seems to take a position that is slightly opposed to that of Izetbegovic. How can you take a position that is slightly opposed to that of Izetbegovic. How can you explain these different positions taken on the one hand by the military and on the other hand by the politicians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't, I'm afraid, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you. Precisely because you are defending your standpoint, and I appreciate this, the standpoint expressed in your reports, it's my task to show you some things that are different from what you said. I wish to point out two more details from this interview. Could we scroll down to the very end of the page. Yes. Thank you. I will read the last part. You'll probably be able to find it where Mr. Halilovic criticises the control of the international community from the very beginning of the conflict, and he says: "If Europe doesn't change its attitude, we will take measures and initiate terrorist actions on their territories. Many European cities will burn in flames. They have tied our hands and feet before an aggression of an army that we used to finance." This is referring to the Serbian aggression. And then, when speaking of the troops in Bosnia up the United Nations flag, Commander Halilovic carefully distinguishes between the behaviour of individual countries and says: "The Spanish Battalion are behaving properly. The French, however, are clearly helping the aggressor and 60 per cent of the soldiers of the Canadian contingent are of Serbian origin. There's no need to comment any further." This last part of Mr. Halilovic's statement shows that throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina, people thought that some people from some countries were showing certain sympathies or certain prejudices towards the different nations. Did you come across that during -- in the course of your work?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did come across a different interpretation of situations between some of the United Nations battalions, yes. I cannot account for the comments made in the interview here. They're very interesting.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I wasn't asking you about other missions such as the UN. I meant to ask whether there was any prejudice within your mission with respect to the members of the particular armies.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it would be correct to say that there were some sympathies, some natural sympathies, between some of the national contingents. I do not believe that they played out in practice. There were, during most of our meetings, monitors from at least three countries present, usually more in the region of five or six.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you tell me whether at any point you had open complaints from anyone within the European mission, complaints about partiality in your reports or accusing only one side in certain situations?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. In particular, I remember a discussion in the Hotel I Zagreb, where I think if my memory is correct, the Greek delegation questioned our analysis and the difference between that and what media was reporting. I think in the end we were able to demonstrate that actually our reporting was correct in terms of the facts and analysis and that media were wrong on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Could we take a look at Prosecution document 52051. In these documents, while we -- which we have, there were at least two such challenges, but let's look at this document, 2051. P 2051. If we can look at the date on the first page. This is a document dated the 1st of May. Let's look at page 1. But I wish to refer to something on page 2 under point 3. Can we see point 3? Yes. "The head of the Zenica regional centre who together with General Morillon, headed the negotiations between the HVO and BH, on the conclusion of the cease-fire agreement 10 days ago, has summed up his observations on the conflict between the HVO and the BH in the report enclosed on the situation in Central Bosnia. He places responsibility for the conflicts that arose squarely on the shoulders of the Bosnian Croatians. ECMM HQ did not endorse HRC/Zenica's desire to lift the arms embargo imposed on the Muslims ..." Do you remember this?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Could we say that this is another example of your receiving a direct challenge to what was stated in the reports?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the letter speaks for itself. It says that there is a difference of opinion on the raising of sanctions. That's a policy issue. It has nothing to do with analysis or matters on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: The report I just showed you was referring to a report compiled on the 1st of May. If we could look at the document 2168. It's also dated the 1st of May. 2168. 2168, the 1st of May, 1993. Could we look at the last page, please. Is this the last page? Is this the report that the previous document was referring to? Let's see who signed it. "If such political action is not possible, the only just solution would be lifting the arms embargo, at least for defensive weapons." All this places responsibility exclusively on the Croats. It's a report by Mr. Thebault, who justifies everything that the Muslim forces have done. He says they're acting out of desperation, because these desperate conditions of living explain the return to religion even of old communists. And he places the blame entirely on the Croats. And then there was a response by Christian Warming. Is this the situation that this report refers to, saying that the lifting of the arms embargo is not something that can be agreed to?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So except for what you said a moment ago, and I have a note written down where you say that later on your analysis showed that you were right, although that should be the subject of examination for which I unfortunately don't have time. So these were two situations --

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must point out that that was referring a different incident. It's not the same matter. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. That's what I said. This is another case, a different incident. The other one was a different one, and this is a different one where we see open lack of agreement. Now, we spoke about the ultimatums yesterday. I have my main topic and my subtopics, and I'll try to get through all of them. I'm afraid I won't be able to do that, but can we see 2D 00090 as the next document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, with respect to the question that was just asked, the last paragraph of the document signed by Mr. Thebault seems to indicate that there was a political drive towards Croatia and the Croats of Bosnia, but that if ever that political action was not crowned with success, then a solution would be -- that would be effective was to lift the embargo on defensive weapons firstly. So was that the ECMM's position as far as a solution was concerned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, thank you. There were a number of solutions suggested. This is a message sent by, I must be careful of my words here, but a desperate ambassador seeking a solution to a desperate situation. We were asking for a number of measures to be taken on both parties to restrain them at a time when conflagration in the area seemed almost certain. That is not fighting in some areas but fighting across the areas. This was one solution from a man within the area. There would, of course, have been other options available to politicians and diplomats outside the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Counsel Nozica.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I asked for a document linked to the ultimatum. Let me repeat the number of the document. It is Defence Exhibit 2D 00090. This is a document of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Ministry of Defence. The date is the 21st of January. It is signed by the minister. The Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Ministry of Defence. Now, you spoke about an ultimatum linked to January, 1993, yesterday, and in response to Mr. Karnavas's question you said you never saw it. Now, I'd like to ask you -- or I'll read it out. I'll read the order out. It says: "Deadline for the order of the 16th of January, 1993, to be completed determined for January the 20th at 2400 hours is extended until the end of the peace talks in Geneva." And it is signed by Minister Bozo Rajic and it was delivered to the Main Staff of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska, the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia- Herzegovina, the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, UNPROFOR, the ESMM in -- with its HQ in Sarajevo. Have you ever seen this order or command as it says? Were you aware of its contents if you hadn't actually seen the order?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had not seen the order, and I was not aware of its contents.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I would now like to go back to a question -- well, in your statement, or in an ECMM report of yours and it was Prosecution Exhibit P 02620, refers to Mr. Stojic directly. And since I have very little time left -- 2620 is the number. It is a report -- yes, that's the report. Can we take a look at point 4, please. Second paragraph, point 4. Second paragraph of point 4. It is the last sentence, in fact, and it says: "The HVO -- the office of the HVO minister of defence, Mr. Bruno Stojic, has and is frequented by arms salesmen, many of them from Germany." That is your report. Do you remember? You signed it.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you explain to us on what basis you were able to conclude, because you said you had five meetings with Mr. Stojic, how were you able to conclude what you did, make these conclusions? What grounds? Did you see those people? Did you meet those people? Did you talk to these people, or did somebody else give you information to that effect?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: In visits to Mr. Stojic's office, I saw people. I saw boxes of equipments. I asked people accompanying me, some of them Croat, afterwards who these people would be, and that is the basis of my report.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understood you fully. The people who brought the boxes were Germans, were they?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was explained to me by people I asked afterwards that they were.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I don't understand. I apologise. You saw some people, and somebody told you that they were selling arms, arms salesmen, and then they brought these boxes full of arms on the spot. Doesn't that seem a little improbable during a time when there was an embargo in force that somebody should come and see the minister directly with boxes, openly shows the contents of those boxes? And let me remind you that you said they had come previously as well and that most of them were from Germany. So this is a definite finite verb, that you draw the conclusion that they came previously, that they came on that occasion. So did somebody tell you about that every time, or did you see for yourself that that was indeed the case?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I hope there's nothing lost in translation here. I did not suggest that they bought arms and sold them on the spot. I said that when I visited that office I saw people. I saw boxes. I asked other people afterwards who these people may have been, and I was told by those people that they were German arms salesmen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: If I may. You seem to assume that the boxes held weaponry. What is this assumption based upon? Were there labels, or were they open?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, they looked like munitions boxes. They were of a certain pattern of wood and paint that suggested they were munitions boxes. And I asked people afterwards who those people may have been. I understood the replies to be that they were German arms salesmen. I'm sorry, I cannot give you better definition of that. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. I know those boxes, so I can understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Beese, you who were a British army officer and who went to the famous academy at Sandhurst, a professional like yourself, if he sees arms boxes, can he not identify the origins, whether they were munitions from the United States, for example, or from Russia, or from Germany, or from France, Great Britain, or whatever else? Those boxes of munitions, as a technician, where would you say those arms came from? Because the salesmen might have been German, which doesn't mean to say that the munitions were from Germany necessarily.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, thank you. I take your point precisely. I was not able to tell at the distance where they came from. I would have liked to have been able to, but it was not -- it was not protocol for us to probe and poke what was happening. We asked questions afterwards. In the same way we had to be extremely careful about asking questions and endeavouring to inspect the presence of foreign troops on the soil, whether they came from Croatia, from the Middle East. These were delicate matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Counsel Nozica.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: However, although according to what you've just explained Their Honours there was absolutely unreliable information, you say at a distance. Well, what distance was this? Because I saw boxes like that during the war, too, but what was the distance that you couldn't read what it said on the boxes? If you enter an office, and we have had occasion to see it, then there's no great distance there from which you would not be able to see the writing on the boxes. So you didn't see the contents of the boxes. You weren't able to establish where the boxes were from. You just said that you heard somebody else say that these were arms salesmen and that they were Germans at that, and then you put all this down as a fait accompli in your report. You don't say alleged or leave a little leeway there, you just put it down as something that is very exact and correct. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the context of this report, which covers HV involvement in Bosnia-Herzegovina, I couldn't either tell you whether a T-55 tank had been made in any one of the East Bloc countries if I was standing next to it. The report covers the presence of foreign arms and a supply of them into the country. If that report by me in connection with this is incorrect and they were not German arms salesmen, I apologise. It doesn't change the weight of the report.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Beese, it is not my intention to enter into polemics, nor can I do that in the court, but I'm just saying that you wrote down something in your report that you did not check out 100 per cent, which you could have done. When you speak of the presence of foreign arms, you spoke in fact of the presence of elements of the Croatian army on the territory -- on HVO territory, and you spoke about licence plates on cars, on vehicles. Can you tell me whether any -- there is any difference between the licence plates that the HV had and the HVO in colour, shape, or any other particularity?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Ms. Nozica, you have said you didn't want to be polemic. Now you tell the witness that he did not control elements that he could have controlled, but he has just said that he could not. So on what do you base the assumption that he could verify more exactly what ammunition was in the boxes and where it came from? He said he could not, and you have not contradicted it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it is not my intention to deny something that is a notorious fact. If the witness says that at that distance he couldn't read what was written on the boxes, it seems logical that if you enter this in your report, you could approach the box and take a look. And also, it is logical -- well, the witness is sticking to his guns. He stated that quite clearly. But I consider that my conclusion, my final conclusion was a logical conclusion to be drawn from the witness's answer. So the first pocket was to draw closer to the boxes and have a look. The second possibility was to try and see the contents in some way. And the third possibility was to talk to the people, which I would have done, although I don't have much experience as an operative. But I would have spoken a few words with those people and tried to see where they were from, what language they spoke, then once I had done that this would have given me more or less reliable material to be able to make that kind of conclusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: So you reject the witness's statement that such control was outside protocol within the context of his mission. You say that is not true. There was no such restraint. He could have -- contrary to what he says, you tell him that his mission, in fact, allowed him to approach the boxes, to inspect them, apparently.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't think that the mission is important here. We know what the mission was. But if this kind of conclusion is drawn and placed in a report without routine verification of the type that I mentioned, I didn't say that the mission had the right to examine the contents of boxes, but just routine control, routine checks that could have been done, then this is an assumption, and it is my job to do that, to challenge what is stated and to establish whether what was written down was done on the basis of research or just on the basis of assumptions. And it is my conclusion that the witness's conclusion was made on the basis of an assumption. I can see that the witness has raised his hand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you may permit me, Your Honours. To understand the seriousness of the situation here, when one of our vehicles closed in on a truck with HV plates and endeavoured to photograph it, our vehicle was fired upon by the occupants. That is the type of action I cautioned our teams not to undertake. This energetic and enthusiastic team did. That is the seriousness with which these issues are dealt with and the context in which we operated.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I asked you something quite different. What is the difference, do you remember, whether there was any difference and, if so, what difference to the best of your recollection existed between the licence plates on HVO vehicles and HV vehicles? That was my question.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I recall correctly, because I myself observed one, HV vehicles had "HV" on the plates. HVO had "HVO."

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Was there any difference in colour between the licence plates?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I recall.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'd like to show you now three examples of licence plates. This is a Mostar licence plate. I'll show you first and then the Trial Chamber after that. These are HVO licence plates. Do you remember them being like that? Yes?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On civilian vehicles. And the HVO plate looked similar to a military vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: What were they like on military vehicles then?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Similar to the HVO plate you've just shown me.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: What do you mean similar? Can you explain that, please?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I can only say similar because it was not possible to draw that close or to photograph, and I'm afraid after 13 years, I can't recall the minor details.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Were they similar in colour?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'm going to show you HVO [sic] licence plates now. This is what they look like. HV. I'm sorry, I made a mistake. I meant to say HV.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then I think we're agreed.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Is this similar, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I replied to your question that HVO plates had "HVO" on them and HV had "HV." That is what you're showing me.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: But you said they were the same colour too.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: They were the same colour, you mean?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have also been careful to say that over 13 years it's difficult to recall. When I came up behind an HV vehicle, I was satisfied it was an HV vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Beese, but I'm going to conclude that it is much easier to recognise licence plates by their colour and if you're close up rather than the letters. Here we can see that the colours of these licence plates are quite different, which can be distinguished and must have been seen at any distance. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not going to dispute that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Then we'll move on to another topic. I don't have many topics left. This next one seems to me to be very important. May we briefly take a look at document 2D 00111, 111. 00111. It is a report of your mission, and it is Prosecution number -- Prosecution Exhibit -- just to mark the document, it is P 03031. Perhaps we'll find it easier that way. Yes. Can we zoom in to where it says M2. This is a report of the 30th of June, 1993. As far as I can see, it is the coordinating centre of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Stop, please. The registrar has just told me that this is a confidential document placed under seal. So we will have to go into private session to discuss it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're back in open session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: May we look at the last page, please. The last page of this document. This is the penultimate. The number is 0737. 0737. The ERN number, I can't see that. I can read it out while we get it up on our screens. I assume we've all seen it. Their Honours have one. "The attack of the army, we think, was an attack to survive the very poor situation on the eastern side and to raise morale. On the other hand, it looks like a first step of linking up the Jablanica area with the Mostar area." Do you remember that report? It's a report of the same day, the 30th of June. Can you confirm whether you remember this report and whether you remember the event as well?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I'm not going to show any more documents. All I want to do is to ask you in conclusion whether in your work in compiling your reports travelling around the terrain, did you ever come across prisons where Croats were incarcerated, and do you happen to remember whether you took part in compiling reports either personally or in the manner in which you explained to us yesterday about prisons in which there were Croats precisely at the period we're discussing, that is to say, the period of your mission in January to the 21st of July?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe we reported that there were prisons holding Croats in the Konjic area.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Did you establish that there were prisons with Croats? I'm asking you personally. Because I looked through large number of documents, and I came across this fact about a prison in only one document. So did you tour the area, learn about this and write about it or take part in writing any document about prisons in which Croats were being held? Mostar, for example. Do you know that there was a prison in the SDK in the Razvitak department store and in the brotherhood and unity school in Mostar? Did you know about prisons of that type in the material period?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did hear there were such prisons, and in discussions with fellow agencies, in take United Nations high commissioner for refugees and the International Committee for the Red Cross, it was agreed that they were primarily their responsibility. They had better and more continual access. Therefore, they would monitor them for the international community, not us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: May I? Thank you for waiting. I simply would like to indicate that the French translation just finished when I started to speak, so it is almost five minutes when the French translation can follow you, and it is -- it is already -- time and again I try to ask all of you, Defence and the witness, et cetera, and even it goes for ourselves, for the Judges as well, and the Prosecution, that really we have to be careful when we are talking. I know that the Defence is in a hurry. I understand this, but it is for everybody's interest that all of us could follow the translation in time. So it is my penultimate request to you. Probably I will repeat it again and again. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours. Your Honour is right. This number of reports and of topics, the number of times the witness has mentioned my client during his examination-in-chief, all of this means that I am under tremendous pressure of time. That is the only reason why these situations arise.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Before His Honour's intervention, you said that you left it to other missions to deal with the prisons in which Croats were imprisoned. Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a general rule, yes. On occasion, we were asked specifically to investigate reports of Croat detainees, and I can think of one in particular, and that is group of Croatian nuns who were said to be imprisoned in the Konjic area. We did investigate to the best of our ability, and we found them to be in good health. On the other hand, when we asked for access to Muslim detainees in Sovici and Doljani area, we were refused access to them. So it is a difficult business inspecting prisoners, especially when you're denied access.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: The Court will have an opportunity to familiarise itself with every report that is admitted into evidence. In quite a few of these you mention visits by your mention to the Heliodrom, and I see in this a discrepancy between what you just said, that you left this to others, but let me ask you a brief question. Did you know that in Zenica, where the regional centre was, there were about a hundred Croats imprisoned in the music school from January to April, 1993? Did you know about this, and did you report this to anyone, or do you know that somebody else reported it?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware of it, and I understand that a number of agencies other than ourselves also understood that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Was this included in your reports? This is the period from January until mid-April, 1993, while you yourself were there. In the same period, there were 250 civilians imprisoned in Mehurici. In the same period in Travnik, Croatian civilians were imprisoned. There were also some imprisoned in the Seretna hotel. I didn't have time to deal with the document dealing with the detention of the entire HVO leadership in Zenica on the 15th, 16th, and 17th of April, 1992. Did you write any reports, or did your regional centre do so, and do you remember these events? And if these events are true and correct, do they alter the picture that follows from your reports, the impression that everything the HVO says about crimes is pure propaganda, as you said?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will answer that in full. I think it deserves a longer reply than a yes or a no. I cannot pretend, and nor would my colleagues in the mission, that either we had the answers to every problem in the region or the resources to even investigate every matter in the region. Our priority was inevitably to attend to areas of immediate conflict where people were dying by the moment. We were not able to investigate every report of prisons. We did know that prison existed. We simply did not have the resources to attend to them. And that is not to say that we preferred one side or the other, but there were pressing matters to be addressed first. That does not mean I do not have sympathy for people incarcerated.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: A prison implies something similar to what you said, organised crime. A prison is merely a consequence, but everything that happened before that was subject of your reporting. I simply wanted to say that the events that resulted in the incarceration of these people cannot be found in the reports for the period while you were reporting. Thank you very much. I have used up my time. I wish to say at the end, and we shall inform Your Honours of this in writing, I was not able to deal with all the topics I intended to deal with during this cross- examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Kovacic and then Mr. Praljak, who has a number of questions to put to the witness. But first there is a question from the Bench.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, one point of clarification, if I may. When answering the questions put to you by Ms. Nozica about your comment regarding the purchase of weapons by the office of Mr. Bruno Stojic, you stated that during one of your visits you noticed a number of boxes, and you assumed that these were boxes containing ammunition. In that office, you also saw people who, according to your information, might have been of German nationality. Conclusion: This was an example of import of weapons, of purchase of weapons despite the embargo. I'd like to know the following considering your experience and your background: I'd like to know if your conclusion related to the violation of the embargo, I'd like to know if that conclusion is based solely on these boxes in the office and on the presence of these people that you assume are Germans in the office, or whether you had other indicia, other information that were -- that led you to reach that conclusion. Do you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. In reply to that, I can say that the comment I made and which has been questioned in detail is a very minor comment in a much larger report which much larger issues at stake. I hope to have been able to alert my superiors to the fact that arms and people were coming in from outside, and if this was an example, it is a small example against a much larger background.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We have 15 minutes or -- no, 20 minutes before the break. I'm now going to give the floor to the last Defence counsel and to Mr. Praljak if he has questions to put to the witness. Last counsel on our list is Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I ask your leave that my client, General Praljak, begin putting his questions, and then I will put my questions after he does. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Praljak, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. We have been preparing for some 20 days to respond to the examination-in- chief. There is a book with 630 paragraphs containing opinions, assumptions, conclusions preconceived opinions which in our view are erroneous and would require a long, exhaustive and precise examination in order to challenge. Unfortunately, although I have tried and tried to shorten my questions, I don't quite see how this will look. Can we go into private session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We are in open session, and we'll now play a number of excerpts of a DVD. This was requested by the Defence, and namely by Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, you have the DVD number before you and a brief summary of each section. Has this been distributed to Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was distributed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Could perhaps the Prosecution be provided with a copy of this summary?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, you got it. It's one table, one paper. It looks like -- no, sorry, yours was left on the desk. Sorry. I apologise, Your Honour [microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] Where it is evident that members of the Arabic world are present here on the territory of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. Here we are today in Busovaca." "These are the faces of citizens of the state of Iran. They were in possession of guns and other supplies, which is later stated in their statements." "This is for our togetherness." "This is the main BH army staff department in Visoko found with the persons named in the vehicle." "These are tapes containing music." "Fervor for the killing of Allah's enemies who are stronger than they have ever been."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So "Fervor for the killing of Allah's enemies." We can skip over this part now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The United Nations participating in the exchange of Mujahedin taken prisoner.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We can proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Alija Izetbegovic reviewing the troops.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [No interpretation]. [Interpretation] We see children aged under 18.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: It's very difficult for the interpreter to hear Mr. Praljak over the tape -- or the DVD.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All those who were involved in the international network of terrorism have had their names expunged or their faces removed in this way.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Alija Izetbegovic reviewing the Mujahedin troops.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You see the tanks, Mr. Beese?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] President Izetbegovic. This is a review of the 7th Muslim Brigade which we do not consider to be a Mujahedin brigade, but it was very religiously oriented with respect to their combat activities.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. Beese, what this greeting means?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not specifically, no.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: For your information, these are the five foundations of the Koran, of Islam.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They are greeting Allah, not the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Thank you. We can move on. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Beese, would you be surprised if I were to say that the UK and half of Europe is trembling before people like these?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: We didn't find this in your reports, Mr. Beese.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must reply I wasn't presented with it by you either.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Beese.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Since there are 40 DVDs that we've supplied to the Court, all testifying -- or 98 per cent of them speaking differently to what we find in Mr. Beese's descriptions, I'd like to show you some and talk about them after the break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. But go ahead and ask your question which summarises what you've just been saying, because during the cross-examination, the witness -- the cross-examination was different, but the witness can now answer your questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the witness wrote 630 points about all this. Now, I don't want to enter into polemics with the witness, but if you give me the time to do so, ten hours, then I'm sure we would have an exhaustive discussion and a useful one. But unless I enter into polemics, I can do nothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'm going to sum up. Mr. Beese, you've just seen several minutes of excerpts from DVDs. Now, with respect to what you might have written in your reports or writings, what is your point of view today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, at the time, the matter of Mujahedin -- [French on English channel]. Sorry. I'll start again, Your Honour. With regard to the Mujahedin, the matter was only ever brought to our attention as a mission when we were present in HVO offices to present a complaint about something else. It was as if it was the primary excuse for the HVO aggression. We were ever available to the HVO at almost any level for them to have presented a case. You can imagine if we had been presented with significant information on either the threat or the outcome of the threat, that we would have passed it to a good number of authorities well beyond us. As it was, we were not presented with this information. As regards the practical part played by, call them Mujahedin for useful purposes, there are others much better qualified than I serving in the mission who could comment on their practical application on the battlefield. I do, Your Honour, find this DVD very interesting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We'll continue in a while, after the break. I saw Mr. Mundis on his feet, but he'll tell us after the break what he wants to say. It is ten to 4.00. We reconvene at approximately ten minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have an hour and a half left to complete the cross-examination by Mr. Praljak and his counsel, but Mr. Mundis was on his feet a moment ago. Let's hear what he has to say. Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I will be as -- as brief as possible and as quick as possible, but I do want to put on the record a number of -- of points at this stage. The first, and again I won't belabour it because I mentioned it yesterday, the first is that the Prosecution remains amenable to agreed facts concerning a number of issues pertaining to the Mujahedin. Second, the Prosecution is of the position that until or unless one or more of the Defence teams can articulate a reason as to why all of this evidence concerning the Mujahedin is relevant, it remains just that, irrelevant to the charges that these six accused face as listed in the indictment. And third, and most immediate in light of the current cross- examination, the Prosecution submits, with all due respect to the accused Praljak, that this is not the proper way to conduct a cross-examination. It's simply showing the witness a -- an excerpt of approximately 38 minutes, according to the sheet that I was provided with a few moments ago, and then asking him some questions about what's contained in 38 minutes of videotape excerpts is not a proper way to proceed on a number of grounds. First of all, we don't know where these videotapes came from, the dates the videotapes were taken, the location where the videotapes were taken, et cetera. And we could suggest that there are ways to proceed if this witness is to be cross-examined on these issues, but the way that -- that General Praljak is doing so in terms of making speeches or making comments is not an appropriate way to proceed. And again, for the record, we, at this point, want to indicate these three points. I am confident that they will continue to -- that they will continue to be raised, but nevertheless at this point in the proceedings which is the first time where it appears as though extended discussions and conversations and evidence concerning the Mujahedin will be led we want to put it on the record, that we think it is irrelevant, that we nevertheless would be prepared to agree to many of these things if the Defence would propose in writing some stipulated facts, but more particularly at this point, we don't believe that the procedure that is -- that has been undertaken is a proper one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may be heard very briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to suggest since this discussion could take a lot of time, as the Prosecution has said he's only saying it for the record, so shall we leave that debate until later on when we tender exhibits, and Praljak will say why he considered it necessary to the videos and what link they have to the testimony and the material shown.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in the indictment, paragraph 17, 37 and 39(a), with respect to joint criminal enterprise, mention is made that we spoke about the -- that we used the -- spoke about the Mujahedins and accuse them, and the Mujahedins are mentioned. Therefore, the Mujahedins in all their dimension, their numbers, their extremist opinions, their religious character, and their brutality and numbers, the way in which they arrived, and then that they went all over the world, and these same people, and I have proof of this, took part in New York, in the events in New York. And that is so important that I don't think we can avoid them today, nor could we have avoided them before. So I rely on -- refer to P 2868, a Prosecution Exhibit on the same topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. Praljak. So when we said it was irrelevant, you're saying that paragraph 17, 37, and 39(a), in your opinion, relate to this problem, and as far as you're concern, it is very useful in your defence case to raise the issue. Is that how we're to understand it? And, Mr. Kovacic, are you going to analyse the problem in that light in a judicial manner?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. In those paragraphs and in some other paragraphs in the indictment and other documents introduced through this witness, mention is made of the Mujahedin as a category and as the product of HVO propaganda, among other things, for the HVO to win over the Croatian people, which according to the Vance-Owen Plan would come under the Muslim side, that those Croats be resettled into other areas which would come under Croatian control according to the Vance- Owen Plan. And we can present arguments to evidence that. So in that context it is highly relevant. And there's another important context, and I have to put my strategy before the witness, but I'm willing to run that risk. The fact is, Your Honours, that the ECMM, in its reports, is minimising -- minimised the existence of the Mujahedin as a factor to be reckoned with in the area. What we wanted to show is that it was an elephant on the road that was bypassed by the ECMM who refused to see this enormous elephant on the road.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, do you want to ask Mr. Beese any questions?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Beese, do you know when the first Mujahedin began to arrive in Bosnia-Herzegovina? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Do you know in 1993, according to internationally relevant sources, how far the ECMM knew about their numbers and what their numbers were in Konjic and in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think we knew, no.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The number that is mentioned in relevant documents is 5.000. Thank you. Now, may we see the next document, and I'll tell you what it's about. They are the names and surnames --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, no objections which are not focused. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I would like to see the document that makes reference to 5.000 Mujahedin in Konjic and Mostar. If that document could be produced, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not in Konjic and Mostar but the total number in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And among other things, in Mostar and Konjic as well, but the figure refers to the whole area.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes. May we have the next document, the names and surnames of those from the Mujahedin ranks from other countries who had to leave Bosnia-Herzegovina under pressure from a major world power. Of course, when the problem of the Mujahedin began to affect it after that famous 9/11 date in New York. A little slower, please. Now, Mr. Beese, do you recognise any of these people? Did you ever meet any of them?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, where does the document come from?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It comes from official but not public sources. And because they are secret services, the secret services of several countries, in fact, and certain persons from Bosnia and Herzegovina as well, I would not like to mention any names, because I could put their lives at risk.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but, Mr. Praljak, the document was handed to you either by Croatian secret services or Bosnia-Herzegovina or some other country, whatever, but you say that you cannot tell us who gave you these documents because you don't want to imperil the source; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this document was compiled -- may we go into private session for me to give an explanation, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After public pressure --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're in open session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, out of an abundance of caution, I would strongly suggest that this material not be made public at this point in time and that it be placed under seal, if Mr. Praljak is intending on exhibiting it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Very well. Now go ahead and ask your question, Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like 3D 00322 to be played now, please, the next document. Your Honour, I prepared the document, which deals with 22 municipalities in which, from Central Bosnia towards Mostar, Mr. Beese moved around and in which there were conflicts between two sides and even three sides. The document was the result of a lot of information and facts and figures, and it enumerates crimes against Croats from 1991 to 1995, crimes committed against the Croats. This is the document. Unfortunately because of the time constraints, I have selected only Konjic. So may we see the Konjic document, please. In the Konjic municipality in a brutal manner, 85 persons were massacred in the following places: Gostovici, Gorani, Boksevica, Trusina, Radesine, Celebici, Orahovica, Zabrdge, Polje Bijela, Spiljani, Ovcari, Galjevo, Ovcari, Podorasac, Vrci, Gornja Visnjevica, Orliste, Mrkosovice, Buscak I and Junkici. May we have the next page, please? Mr. Beese, these are the dates and the names of the victims will be published later on. Next number, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Again, Mr. President, is this a question that's being put to the witness? We would object to this type of procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I assume that Mr. Praljak will get to a question eventually, but before he asks his question he wants to show the witness the document. He can't ask the question before he shows the witness the documents.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. How can I put my question to the witness if, in the words of Mr. Beese, published in his reports, I do not juxtapose this with documents challenging and denying those reports? If I ask him about his reports, I'll receive the same words coming from him that he used in writing his report, and that's quite normal.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: On the 25th of March, 1993, Orliste, four victims, on the 23rd of March, 1993, Vrci, 9 victims. Buscak, the 13th and 14 it is of April, Gostovici on the 23rd of March, 1993, 4 victims. Next page, please, we can skip over the rest. Yes, it's easy for us to skip over the dead. Let's look at Trusina. On the 16th of April, 1993, 23 victims. Those are all the persons who at that point in time were in the village. I'd like to highlight the date, the 16th of April, which is when the crime in Ahmici took place. Ahmici rightly became a symbol of crimes committed by somebody belonging to the Croatian people, but Trusina don't exist anywhere. You won't find Trusina in anybody's report, including your own, Mr. Beese. Isn't that right? No mention of Trusina. Yes or no? As far as your report is concerned.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't get into that area because of your people. So I didn't know. So the answer to your question is no.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next, please. Take a look at the dates to save time on reading them out. Their Honours will be able to read your reports, and they will be able to see that you went to Konjic regularly, and even on one occasion you returned the buses, sent the buses back in order to retain your neutrality. Buses which were supposed to have pulled out the Croats from Celebici, for example, take them back. And your words were that they would be completely safe there. Now, what kind of safety and security existed in Konjic with 17 -- where the Croatian population numbered 17 per cent is something that these documents show. Thank you. And now the last part. On this document, we can see the municipalities that were dealt with in the broader document, and the total number of victims is 1.148 outside combat activities. That is to say, not killed in combat operations. May we now see just one more page. For compiling this presentation, the following material was used: Books, documents, et cetera. They're all publicly accessible, of course, through the engagement of my own team. Thank you. In one point of your report, and because I'm going through this very quickly I haven't found it yet, but anyway, Mr. Beese, you were in charge, among other things, of taking care of - it is paragraph 34 - of the social and economic activities. Death is certainly a social activity, at least where the spirit is concerned. Fear, pain, hatred, sadness, especially when the number of victims is over a thousand. On the territory which at that time was no longer populated by 180.000 Croats. So as a piece of information for the Trial Chamber and you, I have some calculations to show you. Can we show it on the overhead projector, please, on the ELMO? Can we display this document? Can we zoom in on the whole page so we can see the whole page. The whole page, please. Zoom out so we can see the whole page. Thank you. This is mathematics, the arithmetic of death, which is taught in primary school. They are divisions, multiplications, additions and subtractions, and what I calculated is the following: If you take 180.000 inhabitants, and we have 1.184 victims, or 1.200, both civilians and prisoners, then calculated on the example of France that that is a population of 60 million or the United Kingdom which also has roughly 60 million, a population of 60 million, this would be 400.000 dead, the ratio. If we look at the United States of America, then that proportion would be 2 million victims, 2 million persons dead, just on that basis. So my question to you is as follows: For social and economic reasons, did you ever ask yourself what the social psychopathology was of the people, of a people with so many dead? If we were to compare this to America, that would be 2 million dead, killed outside combat. Or in France or in the United Kingdom, this figure would be 400.000 dead, proportionately, let alone the situation that prevailed in our country with no electricity, supply difficulties and so on. Did you look at that kind of psychology and the psychological problems that this led to? Because I never saw anything of the kind in any of your reports. You didn't deal with anything like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Beese, would you answer the question, please. The accused has just told us that on the basis of his calculations, there was 1.184 victims outside combat for a global population of 180.000, and he was drawing a parallel with other countries such as France, Great Britain, and the United States if they had the same number of victims proportionate to the number of inhabitants. So I'd like to refine that question further and say: How come in your reports you make no mention of the importance of those victims and how this was reflected on the population concerned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, to us, any death was a concern, and actually, 5, 10, 15, 20, is significant, but ultimately it's still death. Where we had reports of death or issue, we endeavoured to look into it. We had relatively few resources. Sometimes we had reports of massacres, and we simply couldn't enter the area. We much regret this. Any of us would. But I can't quite see what the point is here, Your Honour. Perhaps I'm missing something. But to us, any death is a concern. And I constantly hear reference to my reports about how I don't report something for one side and do for the other. I think if you look through my account, I make reference to the actions of both sides. If, for instance, there was extreme activity on one side, you will find a reference to extreme activity on the other side. I would like to have investigated more of these issues, but fundamentally our mission was to attempt to dampen the conflict that gave rise to the incidents rather than, as a police force, respond to every one. In the same way as while the United Nations forces faithfully recorded every impact of shell-fire, our concern was: Why are these shells being fired now at this place and what does it mean? So I apologise if we seem to have paid insufficient attention to the casualties. That was not our intention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Mr. Beese, I would like to ask a question. In your previous answer when you answered to Mr. Praljak to a certain question, you mentioned that you were not allowed to go to certain places if you wished to go there, and you were prevented to do so by, in your words if I remember well, that "It was prevented by your own people," you said to Mr. Praljak. So my question is if you were really prevented to go anywhere in your -- in your region of duty. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, we were prevented from entering the area immediately west of Jablanica where we understood that there were problems which needed urgent attention. In the same context as the bus incident referred to earlier, how could we accept when we had established a joint commission of the two sides, Muslim and Croat, that the commission was permitted by one side to enter some areas but not by the other? We had to maintain a neutrality, and we had to encourage, perhaps even coerce, force, other sides to permit us access to territory. It simply wasn't possible. There were times -- sorry. I'm going too fast I expect. There were times when people expected us to investigate an incident and we simply couldn't leave a tunnel without receiving tank fire. This was a very serious business, and we could but complain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we had time, Mr. Beese, I would go through each of your visits to Konjic when Pasalic or Zulfikar Zukaneda [phone] were there and so on, but unfortunately we cannot deal with this fully today. Your Honours, Evan F. Kohlmann after the archives of the secret services of the CIA and others were made public, wrote a book entitled "Al Qaeda's Jihad in Europe, the Afghanistan Bosnian network." It's exhaustive, precise, full of information. So let's take a look at who Mr. Coleman is. Mr. Coleman is an advisor in the United States Justice Department and the FBI for international terrorism. With reference to his book, Mr. Clark of the US Security Council says Coleman's knowledge of this stage of the war on terrorism is complete. And the Prosecutor, in a case concerning the attempt to destroy the VTC in 1993 says that Coleman is one of the leading world experts on terrorism and that he documents this topic in-depth and very knowledgeably. I have prepared 25 points, but there is no chance time-wise. However, let's look at point 16, for example. This is 45 in English. Could you display it for the Judges, please. "As a cultural advisor of Sudan in Vienna in March 1992, Hassanei unofficially had the duty of overseeing the external policy of the MIF in eastern Europe." The MIF is a humanitarian aid organisation. "In an interview given in the 1994, he explained that the issue of the war in Bosnia did not boil down just to making peace or repelling the attacker. Instead, he claimed, "And I quote, "Bosnia must ultimately be Muslim Bosnia. If this does not happen, everything will be pointless and this war will have been for nothing." Your Honour, this gentleman, Hassanei turned up in Zagreb at a humanitarian convention of Muslim countries to provide assistance the Muslims in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Could we now look at 17 or English 46.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please ask a question to Mr. Beese in relation to point 16 on page 45 of the book. What question do you want to put to the witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: My question is the following: Nowhere in his reports have I seen a clear explanation of the ideology that was so present of 5.000 Mujahedin who were in Bosnia-Herzegovina then. How is this represented in his reports? How can you explain this to me?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: On one occasion related in my account, I describe how the mayor of Visoko asked me to view a video of immense concern to him and of concern to me. I do not recall any occasion where the HVO attempted to present in any formal way their concerns. If we were unaware, I apologise, but --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Praljak. You are here quoting someone who quotes someone else who is from Sudan. He is not a Bosnian. He is not a Muslim from Bosnia. And I think it's a bit far-fetched indeed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, and I'll tell you why. Because it's only a matter of time, and I cannot read where and when that man said this, it's my inability to bring in four files of documents which this same gentleman was involved in the financing of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina with hundreds of millions of dollars. These documents originate from the Bundesnachrichten Dienst and the German investigation centres as well as the Austrian investigation centres. Therefore, could we look at 17, English 46. This gentleman --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I have to draw your attention to the fact that this is a statement dated 1994. Magazine interview 1994. That is after Mr. Beese's time there. I think you are really stretching our patience very far by bringing forward material that is hardly possible to link to the issues this witness is called to testify about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's try to find a way out of this problem. Don't you want to ask the following question to the witness: It seems that whilst you were in theatre, the presence of some 5.000 Mujahedin was mentioned, and apparently the Defence would try and understand the presence of these 5.000 foreign fighters in Bosnia-Herzegovina were fighting either against the HVO or against the Serbs. Why is the presence of these people not mentioned repeatedly in the various reports you would send to the European mission and to the -- and to the relevant authorities? I think that's what Mr. Praljak is trying to a ask bit clumsily and I'm going to phrase the question myself on my own we behalf. How some these 5.000 foreign fighters were never mentioned in your reports? Can you provide an explanation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, during my time in Bosnia-Herzegovina, I was aware that there were foreign fighters, if we want to call them that, working for both sides, both Croat and Muslim. I did not have specific details and data or numbers for either party's foreign fighters. If there is a suggestion that there were 5.000 foreign fighters working for the Muslims, then that would have been such an enormous issue and problem in terms of effect on the ground that we could not fail to have noticed it. If, however, we had proven there was a gathering of a significant number somewhere, that would have been a matter for the United Nations Protection Force to address. We might have reported on it, but unfortunately, we did not have the information to report upon. And if there is an oversight there on our part, I can but apologise for our mission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, you can proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 46, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: "The TWRA," that's another humanitarian organisation, "was also involved in the procurement and transportation of weapons primarily from Sudan and the former Soviet Union directly to the Bosnian front line. In September 1992, western intelligence officials learned of a major ongoing project of the relief agency to ship 120 tonnes of Soviet-made assault rifles, mortars, mines, and ammunition via Sudan and Slovenia to Muslim forces in Bosnia. After Soviet-built transport planes deposited the arms in a Slovenian warehouse leased by the TWRA, chartered helicopters provided by a joint Russian-American venture shuttled the weapons from the warehouse through Croatia directly to Tuzla and Zenica." Mr. Beese, did you see helicopters used by the army of Bosnia- Herzegovina, MI6 Russian made?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Do you know the number of men under arms in the army of Bosnia- Herzegovina during the time you were in theatre?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Do you know the numbers of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: There was shooting every day, either against the Serbs or against each other for the most part.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
