utterances.text: Can you imagine how many tons of ammunition, shells, and so on were needed every day to be delivered to the theatre for that amount of shooting to take place? How many tons would that be per day in your view?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware before the conflict and before I arrived that Yugoslavia, as an entire nation, had prepared itself for lengthy war. I understood there were stockpiles of munitions all over the country. So I hadn't specifically asked myself, I'm afraid, how many tons had to be brought in to sustain that kind of conflict.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Beese, we have concluded here umpteen times that the JNA, before the conflict began, cleaned out all the depots of the Territorial Defence to the last bullet. Nothing was left, or what was left was so little there had to be truckloads and truckloads of ammunition rolling in from Croatia every week to the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina to make it possible for them to shoot that much. There had to be tank trucks of fuel for tanks to drive around, for helicopters to fly around, and for you to fuel your vehicles. And in your report, you mention two cases which can be used up by five men in one day, five men shooting the way people were shooting there, which you saw with Mr. Bruno Stojic. Allegedly saw. Do you have any explanation for this? What kind of observer were you? What kind of analyst were you? You were someone who was supposed to learn the truth and write about it.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: With respect particularly to HVO resupply, I have commented in my account, and I commented in my official reports that there was an enormous weight of Croatian resupply coming in from Dalmatia. I have commented on helicopters being used by the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina to resupply the enclaves. I have remarked upon the US aircraft that flew below my hotel window to keep Bosnian helicopters on the ground. I have reported these matters.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Beese, please. My intelligence is not so poor. I keep asking you what were 200.000 members of the armija -- army of Bosnia- Herzegovina using to shoot every day at the Serbs or at the Croats? Where were their weapons coming from, from Belgrade by helicopter or from Croatia, breaking the embargo, violating it? And if there was an indictment here for violations of the embargo, we could have thousands of accused here whom we could lock up right away. If we were not to adhere to the principle that no embargo can prevent the natural right of individuals and nations to self-defence once the aggressor from Serbia was not stopped. Where did they get this from? You were on the ground. You walked around. You investigated. It was your duty to investigate things. Do you have any knowledge about this? Just say yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I do not mean to insult your intelligence, and if it comes across that way, I must apologise for that. I do apologise. On the matter of resupply, I have heard claims from the HVO that they resupplied the Muslims for a considerable period during the conflict. Otherwise, I do not have information on resupply, no. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you. And two more points. English 90. Could we have it displayed? Colonel Stjepan Siber, the deputy of the commander of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the operative commander for Central Bosnia boldly stated for the Western press "It was a mistake to allow Arab guerrillas to come here. Nobody asked them to come. They committed the most crimes and they're working against the interests of the Muslim people. They are killing, looting, and stealing. They are not under the control of the army of BH, and they have to leave. We hope that President Izetbegovic will command them within a few days to leave." This is quoted from Andrew Hawk, "The Trail of the Mujahedin." "Rasim Delic, the then-commander of the Bosnian Muslim army admitted that the foreigners were "perpetrating" senseless massacres like their enemies. They are kamikaze, desperate people." Josip Bogdanski, Iranian and Bosnian leaders and so on, 1993, page 6. This was said by those who had a lot more reason to hide the truth about the Mujahedin than a monitor of the European Union would have, and that's what you were, Mr. Beese. I will skip over a vast amount of material concerning Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Praljak. You've just mentioned Colonel Siber quoted by Rasim Delic. What is the question you want to put to the witness in relation what you're trying to establish?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Beese, did you meet Mr. Delic and Mr. Siber and talk to them about these issues, and, if you did meet them, did they answer any questions you may have put to them about the Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met Mr. Delic, on one occasion only, in Jablanica. I met Colonel Siber on a number of occasions in Central Bosnia. The issues we were discussing at the time were, I'm afraid, more to do with HVO aggression into Fojnica than they were about Mujahedin. If I had known more about Mujahedin, I might have asked the questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now move into private session, and I'll have just a few more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we have on the monitor P 3827, that document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I hope it is a public document. I checked that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is a document dated the 30th of July, and we'll see that it is a letter signed by Ambassador Jean-Pierre Thebault, the head of the office in Zenica. I apologise to Mr. Beese. I did not introduce myself, but I assume you've gathered that I am Mr. Praljak's Defence counsel. I omitted it say that.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, here we have an observation. On page 3 -- we see the date here, the 30th of July, 1993. Zenica, HRC. Last page, page 3, please, and the last paragraph on that page. Page 3. Mr. Beese, this is the last portion. Would you read it out, please, the last paragraph? Or, rather, here we see an answer made by your superior, Ambassador Thebault, and according to the date, this was written sometime after you had left. So two or three introductory questions first. We saw earlier on and heard from you that some assertions in the reports were sometimes prepared for several days, because various information came in and then you waited for several days to write something. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It might be possible, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you perhaps take part in any way in the preparation of this piece of information or, rather, did you have information on the basis of which this assessment was made and presented in this document?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I see the date again? I don't think so. Can I see the date again, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The 30th of July, 1993.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I had no part in the preparation of this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Do you happen to know, perhaps, whether Ambassador Thebault talked to General Praljak with respect to his links with the HVO forces or, rather, with Croatia in general?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you know perhaps that Mr. Thebault might have talked to the Defence Minister, Mr. Susak, about the topic?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I know nothing in relation to this subject at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [In English] Okay. [Interpretation] In another document of yours, not to go into private session, you know the one I mean, P 92601, you make no mention anywhere of General Praljak. Did you ever meet him?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Heard anything about him?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Nothing about his role?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll try to deal with an area for which I would need more time, but I'll try and do it in the time I have. May we have document P 2692 placed on e-court, please, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Beese, it will come up soon. It is a report of the ECMM dealing with the events of the 8th of June, 1993. A little lower down, please. We can see the date. Yes, there we have it. It is the 9th of June, 1993. And further down we see that the report covers the 8th of June, 1993. May we now turn to page 5 first, please. Page 5. On page 5, we have a title "Special report, Travnik." The 8th of June, 2006. At the bottom of the page. At the bottom of page 5, please. The bottom of page 5, please. [In English] We lost it from the monitor. [Interpretation] I suggest we put it on the ELMO since it's gone from e-court. At least I can't see it on e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: It's back now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's reappeared. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: As I was saying, the excerpt that we see here, have you read through it, Mr. Beese?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: From this we can see that the ECMM visited the village of Guca Gora. However, you denied that anything important -- any important incident happened in Guca Gora. Now may we look at page 6, and we'll look at a few excerpts there and then I'll ask you some questions. Page 6, please. And at the top we have a paragraph with the heading "Specific." May we zoom down to the next paragraph. Scroll down. Yes, there. Would you read out the paragraph beginning "The armija command were questioned about alleged atrocities ..." ? Would you read that paragraph, please. They offered to visit the village. They did visit it. Mirko Ivkic, from Travnik, a priest was present as was UNPROFOR, and you establish what it says here, that the village was empty. That the were refugees in the church. There was one casualty who was treated there, and that the body of a civilian was found. Were you there visiting Guca Gora yourself?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You were not there. Right. Did you hear anything about this report and that visit and the event? You said you worked as a team when it came to important information.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: On page 7 -- may we see page 7 of this document now, please. After the visit, consistent with what it said, would you read out the first excerpt on the page. Here, in a way you imply that they are rumours here again, which could suggest a coherent and coordinated Croatian policy with careful management of information. So that is your main assessment, the assessment you make in that paragraph. Do we agree?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not write this personally. I do understand the events. I would try to understand what you're saying here. There was a report that the church had been burnt and many civilians killed. The patrol of ours went to the village when they could, found the church was still standing intact, and there was one death. That was not the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. Beese, but we don't have time to go into that. The documents on our screens, we're all able to read it. We know what it says. All I'm doing is putting this to you, that from the parts we have read, it would emerge that throughout the time you considered that it was a minimal event, a minor event. That's the first point. And second, that it was the fruit of propaganda, that the event was an example of HVO propaganda, in fact. Do you agree with that assertion?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had to consider that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: However, I could go on showing you a number of reports, but I'm just going to show for the record page 7, RC Zenica on the 8th of June. Then page 8, and so on. So the assertions are the same all through this report. For example, on page 8, assessment. We have an express assessment on your part here, page 8. Somewhere in the middle it says: "We are witnessing the Bosnian Croat propaganda [In English] is best against the Bosnians which will be difficult to diffuse and to clarify with what really happened." [Interpretation] Now, a question. During your previous testimony, you confirmed that you knew, in fact, you had limited resources and that objectively speaking, it was well nigh impossible to establish the facts and what actually happened -- when you tried to establish what actually happened. Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And you stress that here, that it will be difficult to diffuse and clarify what really happened; right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, I'm going to ask my assistant to play a video now about Guca Gora, because we've just seen --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have four more minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I'm quite sure that will suffice.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: While that's getting ready, Your Honour, by my calculation, Your Honour, for the next witness, I have 25 minutes. I have no intention of cross-examining the next witness, therefore, I would like to donate my 25 minutes of the following witness to the Praljak team so they could complete the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we play the tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: "... where the villages sought sanctuary. Guarded overnight by British warriors which had been driven to their rescue. Inside, 187 Croat men, women and children, too terrified to leave for fear of being slaughtered by rampaging Muslim soldiers. For the British army commander trying to reach Guca Gora the road was fraught with danger and problems. Why don't you help us said this group of Muslims?"

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we stop there?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: We saw the British officer. Do you happen to recognise him? You met him, I think.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid that was a very quick glimpse. I did recognise other people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You'll see him again, and we'll see -- no. We'll see who you recognise in and I'll ask you later?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: "... fear of being slaughtered by rampaging Muslim soldiers. For the British army commander trying to reach Guca Gora, the road was fraught with danger and problems. Why don't you help us, said this group of Muslims who showed him a young boy's body to prove how they were suffering too. Eventually, the reinforcement warriors were allowed to move on after promises that once the Croats had been taken to safety, the British would return to help Muslim people. In Guca Gora, those brave enough to venture outside were preparing to bury their dead. Seven in all killed in yesterday's battle. There was no priest there and so the army chaplain took charge of the funeral service." "The gunmen in the surrounding hills tried to prevent these people from paying their last respects, but as British army snipers took cover, the chaplain read on." "The attack continued until the army replied with 340 rounds from their chain guns. It was then that the commanding officer decided to evacuate the monastery giving orders for the families to be transported inside his armoured warriors. Thank you, they said, as they clutched their children and a few belongings. They were leaving their homes but they were all together. The most delicate of passengers were tenderly hoisted aboard by burly British squaddies. It was the first real test in Bosnia for the man in charge, and it's being regarded as huge success." "If we get these people out we have achieved something. It is a small attempt. And I'm well aware that around this whole area of conflict, there are many other people..." MR. KOVACIC: [Interpretation] We have run out of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The first question, this UNPROFOR official, do you know him?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Alistair Duncan. You met him personally, did you?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: He was at the base in Vitez, was he?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So from this video and from what Duncan says, we saw certain facts. We saw that people were on the run, and in later reports that I won't be able to refer to, you go a step further and accept in the ECMM report number 2849 P, I hope you'll take me at my word, in a later report you accept that UNPROFOR did find six dead bodies, but you still state that all this was propaganda, do you? How can you explain the difference? On the one hand, we saw authentic footage and we saw the intervention by BritBat violating their policy of neutrality, shooting at Muslim forces which are making it impossible for the funeral to take place, and the whole atmosphere shows that Guca Gora was a serious incident, whereas the ECMM reports constantly state that it was nothing more than HVO propaganda. How do you explain that difference?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: You've seen in this video that UNPROFOR was active in the area with significant amounts of armour and men. You also see from the coverage that the church reputedly burnt to the ground is still intact. You also see some members of our team in the background. So we accompanied UNPROFOR. UNPROFOR would have produced their complete report of the patrol. Our comments relate to the allegation that the church was burn to the ground. It was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: We agree. We agree that all the information that went round the international bodies were not correct. I completely agree with that. That's quite obvious. But it is also obvious that the event itself was far more serious than the description or image portrayed on the basis of these ECMM descriptions. And if I were an ambassador of one of the ECMM countries using those reports, had I read the document, just like my colleague said, in a comfortable atmosphere of air-conditioning, listening to light music, quite obviously I did not receive information that in Guca Gora at the same time when the Croats might have committed some crime that simultaneously, the Croats were victims over there and that was the chain of events that's what happened so that kind of information is not contained in your report. Guca Gora was portrayed as primarily an attempt at propaganda. That's the fact as it stands. Do you agree with that or not? I'm not asking for an explanation, I'm just asking you whether you agree with what I'm saying or not. Just give me a yes or no answer. Yes, you agree or no you don't. But your yes and no to the question of whether it is true that your main conclusion about Guca Gora was that it was just purely HVO propaganda regardless of the dimensions of the event. You keep maintaining that it was HVO propaganda, nothing more. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Thank you. Your Honour, I'd just like to assure you, and when we come to proof and evidence, I would have several more examples, if time were to allow, where we have documents and videos that events happened in quite a different way than the ECMM portrayed them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I hope Mr. Mundis does not have any additional questions at this point since the Judges have no questions. We observe that the Defence had nine hours, 17 minutes for the cross-examination. The registrar has put me right. It was 9 hours, 7 minutes, but anyway, it was more than the 8 hours initially stated. Mr. Beese, thank you for coming to testify for the Prosecution. You came twice. We wish you a good return to your country and every success in your future activities. It's quarter to 6.00. We're going to take the usual 20-minute break and reconvene at approximately five past 6.00 when we will introduce the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The hearing is resumed. I see that the blinds are down. First of all, let's stay in open session about the exhibits to be tendered by the Defence. Please wait until tomorrow to tell us about these exhibits, because we have to begin hearing the witness now, and tomorrow at the beginning of the hearing we'll expect you to tell us what exhibits you want to be tendered. Mr. Mundis, if the blinds are down, I suppose that something new has happened. So we'll now move into closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have two very quick matters which can be dealt with while the witness is being brought to court. The first one relates to a future witness, Mr. Mesic. There is a Rule 92 bis motion pending from the Prosecution. Our response is presently due on Friday. We would like to take the weekend to finalise it. Mr. Mundis has kindly indicated that there is no objection from the Prosecution, so I make an oral application for leave to -- for an extension of time until Monday to file that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. Murphy. The Trial Chamber takes note of your application, and it is granted. You will be able to file your missions on Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: The second matters relates to another forthcoming witness, Mr. Tomljanovich. The Chamber may recall that this witness is an employee of the Office of the Prosecutor. We had some discussion about that, and I see Your Honour nodding, so I needn't deal with it at length. We felt it right to draw Your Honour's attention to the fact that the Trial Chamber in the Milutinovic case has made an order with respect to a similar witness that it would not be proper for him to be accepted as an expert witness because of his closeness to the Prosecution team in preparing the case and interviewing witnesses. That -- that issue has apparently -- the Prosecution has applied for certification for appeal of that issue. My understanding is that the Trial Chamber has not ruled on it yet. Clearly, it would be undesirable for there to be conflicting rulings between two Trial Chambers on this point, and we would like to make the suggestion, Your Honour, that perhaps sometime early next week, both the Prosecution and the Defence be permitted to file very brief submissions on that issue to invite the Trial Chamber to reconsider its ruling in the case of Mr. Tomljanovich. This need not delay his testimony in any way, because regardless of the outcome, he would clearly be entitled to testify as a factual witness and the conclusions to be drawn from his testimony by the Chamber would be all that's in issue there. So my application would be to file brief submissions on that matter, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Murphy. This is news to us that the Milutinovic trial in a similar case ruled by saying that a staff member of the Office of the Prosecution could not appear as an expert witness. This order has been -- is on appeal now. A certification has been requested, and you're stating that this could pose us a problem. Tomorrow morning, as usual, we'll have a meeting. We'll discuss that issue, and then we'll let you know what we've decided. We'll let you know whether we maintain the decision we took earlier on or whether we consider that the witness should be heard as any other witness and that his written report should not be admitted. The other question we'll have to rule upon tomorrow is whether you will be allowed, on both sides, to file submissions. But as I'm speaking, I'm looking at the chart here about prospective witnesses. As you know, next week we have one witness who will come to be cross-examined, plus an additional witness, and that person, the one you're mentioning, should be heard the following week. Therefore, this is very short notice. We don't need hours to understand the problem. I've understood within 15 seconds. We'll discuss the matter tomorrow morning, and then we'll let you know about our decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I have one just one brief matter, Your Honour and -- well, just going back to that what -- you could give us until Monday, both sides, to respond since the Prosecution is already aware of the issue, but my -- my matter is, and we could take this up tomorrow at some point after the witness, because we don't intend to cross-examine him. I don't think the witness will be there for a minute or two. But getting back to the assertion that there has been some abuse by some members of the Defence, I take it probably I stand guilty as charged on that for taking more time than necessary, I certainly want to go on record to at least express my profound regret that when we have this strict, you know, sort of stopwatch approach, it is a fundamental unfairness to our clients, and I don't think any one of us who is not an accused would appreciate being tried in this kind of fashion, because tomorrow this witness will probably be ending after the first session and we'll have two additional sessions. But I do want to at least have the opportunity to put on record that I believe that especially with this last witness, no abuse was made by anyone, and that the Trial Chamber, while it has shown flexibility, should perhaps be slightly more flexible in the future on occasion. And I've done this job for a very long time. I certainly can improve. I certainly would like guidance from the Trial Chamber as to how I can improve and be more efficient. But I think just for the record, for every hour of cross-examination, my team spent well over 200 hours in preparation for this witness, and, gentlemen, please consider that. There is no need for me to prepare if I will not have the opportunity to represent my client. He deserves as much as I can give him, as everyone else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: This is an occasion to bring something to your attention that I have been pondering and we have been discussing for some time. First of all, let me say that I fully agree with what you've just said, that you are here for your clients and you must, of course, be able to get the maximum out of the time that is available here. And cross- examination can certainly be a very valuable and important instrument in getting a more complete and correct picture of the realities, also in assessing the credibility of the witness. I want to make it quite clear that this is not in question and that the Chamber is fully in support of this basic idea. I also wish to say that we share, the Chamber shares the bad feelings that the Defence very frequently voices at being in a kind of a temporal corset which, of course, the Chamber has not chosen as the Defence has not chosen. These are circumstances that you cannot completely disregard without not doing our duty. Now, it has occurred to me, especially when re-reading the transcripts after an absence of four days where I could not attend, where I read them particularly carefully that it is a suggestion to you -- of course, it is not for us to tell you how to do your job and I'm again fully aware of that, but it might be of some use if you very critically re-read the transcripts of cross-examinations, so to speak, asking yourself word by word, "Was this necessary?" We have the feeling, and I know my colleagues share this entirely, that a very large amount of words used here are not conducive to the -- to what we conceive as being the usefulness of cross-examination. We have a lot of simple pleading. We have rhetorical elegance, which we do appreciate, but still regard as something of a bit of luxury. We want, if you want to follow my example, to find brilliant examples of economic cross-examination, and you may also find other instances where you might reconsider whether it is impossible to improve the style so as to get more out of the limited time that is at our proposal. I ask for understanding that I make this statement. I regard it myself as delicate. I don't like to -- to do it, but it has occurred to me and I thought it was only a matter of courtesy and honesty that I share the thought with you. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Thank you. I wouldn't like to prolong the discussion on that issue which was raised by Mr. Karnavas, but since yesterday I raised the question of how to cope with the situation that we are of course pressed by time, I do agree, first of all, with the statement just made by -- by Judge Trechsel. Secondly, I would also like to emphasise that we are not and I am not for a kind of stopwatch approach as it was mentioned by Mr. Karnavas, but simply we would like to call your attention to the fact that during the last I would say couple of months after when the decision of the Trial Chamber was adopted on the time sharing, I am -- I'm really sure that the -- the Defence has always had more than the return, I would say, 50 per cent, and I'm sure of it. And now, as we have heard, we had -- I mean -- we heard that nine hours, 7 minutes were used and of course I do not remember exactly what was the chief examination for Mr. Beese, but I'm sure it was less than that. But having said this, again I emphasise that I am fully aware and in a way clinging to the important issue of the Defence's rights, and I will do whatever I can to assure this right to you and to ensure that the Defence should always be listened to adequately. At the same time, I think that what examples were mentioned by Judge Trechsel, they also have to be borne in mind, and I hope that this issue will not have any major -- excuse me, any major repercussions in the future but we can go along with useful work, all of us here in the Chamber. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'll give the floor to Mr. Prlic later. Let me just add that I fully agree with what has just been said by my two colleagues. For me, the actual problem, the real problem you're experiencing is due to the fact that in between yourselves, you don't seem to be able to find an agreement about how to share the time. Let me take an example with this witness, Mr. Beese. We saw that Mr. Ibrisimovic decided that he was not going to ask any questions because this witness was not concerning him and his client, so then you should have been in a position to know who was coming second, third, and fourth, and you should have been able to appropriately distribute the time amongst yourselves, because we had been quite flexible in the time we had allocated to you. We said eight hours, or as the Prosecution, speaking from memory, had used five hours and a few minutes. So we had been extremely flexible in our approach towards you. But despite that, despite these eight hours granted to you, you were not able to find an agreement, because you don't seem to be able to decide who is going to ask that question, who is going to ask that other type of question, because that's the way you would be able to gain time. Let me take an example. The issue of the credibility of the witness. One of you could be the one to deal with the credibility of the witness. There is no point in all four lawyers dealing with that issue. Another example, the HVO, the Mujahedin. That could have been allocated to one of you or several of you. And I think it's because of all these problems that we are faced with the problem we have, because you don't seem to be able to find an agreement. We all agree with what Mr. Karnavas has just said. The Defence is entitled to speak, to ask questions, but we are pressed for time. We have a limited amount of time at our disposal. And do not forget that the objective of the cross-examination is for us to understand the essence of your case. That is your interest. Therefore, the questions you put to the witness have to be extremely focused. What you should ask yourself is, "If I were the Judge, would I find this question interesting?" That's the approach you should have when cross-examining a witness. If you adopt that approach, you will gain time. And that's what Judge Trechsel told you, please read very carefully the transcript of the examination-in-chief in order to focus your questions during the cross-examination. I know that that is very difficult exercise, but we trust you. We believe that you are able to conduct this exercise properly. Mr. Prlic, you wanted to take the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I am not participating in these proceedings, but I do feel the need to say something. As a person who is accused here, I am in favour of shortening the time but under one condition. I am the last person to give advice to Your Honours, but if the proceedings were streamlined in such a way that the important points were clear, cross-examination could be conducted differently. I do prepare for my counsel, and for the first time he was able to use over 50 per cent of what was prepared with the witness. Usually the percentage is about 10 per cent. I feel that this imperils my fundamental rights. We cannot uphold the principle if we don't know what is behind it. We all know this principle of the same amount of time divided by six is not a good one, but there is time limit, there is an indictment, and we cannot influence that. So I would appeal to Your Honours to direct the proceedings more, because the indictment is so wide-ranging with a joint criminal enterprise involved that we have to prove there was another joint criminal enterprise with others supporting it, and this is posing enormous problems for us. My Defence will not be very involved when this comes to the crime base, but we do have to get involved when it has to do with policy and politics and so on. The time could be shortened if Your Honours were to point out what you felt was especially important. Also, we have a proofing chart which is either not adhered to or not used. If we have a witness and we are told he's going to refer to such-and-such counts in the indictment, we should all then adhere to that, and then this would shorten the time, both of the examination-in-chief and the cross-examination. However, we have witnesses talking about all kinds of things. If a witness says there was no telephone, it takes 20 seconds for him to say that. But then if we have to prove to that, in fact, there was a telephone we may need up to three hours to prove that. So I would suggest to the Chamber to suggest at every point what is most important. Also, if the Prosecutor were to state clearly what is the aim the Prosecution which is to achieve through a particular witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Prlic, for these comments. We'll discuss this matter again tomorrow, because you have to understand that this is an issue that we repeatedly discuss during our meetings, and considering the comments made by all of you today, we'll consider the matter again tomorrow in order to try and find a solution that is acceptable for everyone. We don't want the accused to have the feeling that they are not being listened to. We don't want their lawyers to have that feeling either. Mr. Mundis, about that specific issue would you like to say something?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. President, just one point to respond to something that Mr. Prlic just said, which is of potentially of very great importance. Page 82, lines 12 to 14, wherein Mr. Prlic said, "My Defence will not be very involved when this comes to the crime base." I'm just, at this point, signalling to everyone that the Prosecution is going to attempt to re-engage the Defence with respect to perhaps some admissions concerning the crime base, because again as -- even as Mr. Karnavas himself indicated with respect to the following witness, they're not going to be extensively cross-examining that witness, and again, crime base is something that we might be able to save a significant amount of time on were there to be some admissions or were we to be in a position to adduce that evidence by way of additional means. And I'm simply at this point signalling to everyone that we will be re-engaging the Defence on additional issues, particularly relating crime base, as a means of saving additional time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. With your comments you give me the opportunity to say the following -- to ask the following: The next witness was scheduled for -- to take two hours and a half for the examination-in-chief. There are four main points in the examination of the witness, four dates that the interpreter has missed. Mr. Prlic has invited us to direct the proceedings. If it was me, I would not need two hours to cover these four dates. So I'd like to invite the Prosecution to really focus the examination-in-chief on the most vital issues, because as you perfectly well know, what everything you -- you present during your case you find it back in the judgement, but sometimes for one witness you'll have just one footnote at the end of the judgement, because otherwise the judgements would be thousands of pages long. So as far as I'm concerned, I believe that two and a half hours, that's far too long. One of the solutions we could envisage would be to interrupt you, and as Mr. Prlic has quite rightly said, it might be up to the Judges to refocus the proceedings. The Tribunal as a whole is currently considering its completion strategy. There will soon be a Plenary Session of all the Judges of the Tribunal to see how we can achieve that. As far as I'm concerned, and I've made no secret about it, I believe that we would go much faster if the Judges were able to control the proceedings more than they can, but unfortunately we are using proceedings that is now very, very old and where the Judges have to -- can't intervene as much as they should. But the Judges are currently considering these issues, and this might lead to changes in the procedure that would make the proceedings much more efficient. Our objective is for each and every one of you to be able to speak as part of an adversarial -- this adversarial system, and the aim is also for the accused to have the deep feeling that their case has been put properly to the Judges and understood by the Judges, because if that's not the case, then justice cannot have been rendered properly. We have a few minutes left. We've bring in the witness in order to deal with the protective measures, and tomorrow we should complete the testimony of the witness. So I'll ask for the witness to be brought in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, while the witness is being brought in, if I can indicate that at least I intend to conduct the examination-in- 6 chief in much less than two and a half hours, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's very good news. So we've already saved 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: I think we were in open session, Your Honour. Should we perhaps go into private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're in open session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. In open session I give the floor to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Witness, during 1993, around May 1993, your husband, was he a soldier or involved in any military organisation?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: During 1993, May 1993, Dreznica, could that be described as falling within territory controlled by the ABiH or by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: During May, 1993, did you feel safe living in Dreznica as a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And is it correct that you decided to invite your family to come and live with you at that period, or certain members of your family?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Where was your family or these members of your family living in May, 1993?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Prozor, Gracanica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: How far is Gracanica from Dreznica approximately?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Approximately 20 kilometres. 20, 22 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And Gracanica, is that within what can be described as ABiH territory or HVO territory at that stage?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that stage it was HVO, Gracanica was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Which members of your family, without mentioning names, which members of your family were living there at that stage?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were all there. There were no problems at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, but which members of your family were living in Gracanica during May, 1993?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: My sisters and brothers, my mother and father, my daughter-in-law and -- or, rather, yes, my daughter-in-law and her son.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Gracanica at that stage, could you describe or give the Court an idea of how many people lived there and whether they were Muslim or Croat?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And were there more Muslims or more Croats living there?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: More Muslims in that village.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Could you tell the Court why did you think that it would be good to invite your family to come and live with you in Dreznica?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I saw that something would happen. The HVO put up checkpoints in Prozor, in Gracanica, and that's when I went up there to ask them to come down to Dreznica and live with me, especially my father who was an invalid. He didn't have a leg. He didn't want to leave his house nor his property.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: When you went to Gracanica, when was that?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Around the 18th. I can't say exactly. 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And which month?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I can't be sure. I can't remember the month.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: We've been talking about May so far. Would that have been in May?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in May.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Who went with you to Gracanica?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: My husband and I.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: At that stage, that's shortly before the birth of your first son, so you were pregnant at that stage?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that your parents and brothers and sisters, they didn't want to leave Gracanica, so you and your husband, what did you do then?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: We tried to go back to the village of Dreznica. In the meantime, checkpoints were erected and we weren't able to pass because of the HVO army. They didn't allow us to come back down, so I stayed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The checkpoints, by which army were they manned?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The HVO army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did they tell you why you -- why you couldn't leave the municipality or go back to Dreznica?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You and your husband then stayed in Gracanica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Now, during the next few weeks did you become afraid while staying in Gracanica?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Why did you become afraid?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was afraid because of the soldiers. They would go around at night, shoot at houses, make a lot of noise, throw bombs in the forest and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Which soldiers were these?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Soldiers of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And do you have any idea from which unit or from which area these soldiers came?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. All I know is that they were people from Jajce. I remember that well. They didn't do anything to us. They didn't mistreat us or touch us in any way. I know that very well. As to the rest, I know that most of the soldiers were from Papak. They did what they did mostly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Papak, where is Papak situated?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Papak and Gracanica are at a distance of three kilometres roughly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And the people living in Papak, are they Muslim or Croat?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: These soldiers that you refer to who came and who made you afraid in Gracanica, how did you know that they belonged to the HVO?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I knew. I knew that very well, because I would see some of those young men. I recognised them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Were they wearing uniforms?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were wearing camouflage uniforms, multicoloured uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And did they have any insignia?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did. They had HVO insignia on their arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you at that stage know what HVO insignia looked like?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did know. I had seen them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So being afraid in -- in Gracanica, did you stay in Gracanica?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We were in the woods. We might go back and get some food or cook some meals, but we would go back to the woods because we were afraid of staying in the houses and the HVO soldiers turning up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you decided, you and your family, to move away from the immediate area of Gracanica?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no. We stayed there. We didn't have anywhere else to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Now, during June did you go to Mount Tolovac?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, when we come to this piece of evidence, it -- it may be a good time to stop because this will introduce the next phase of the witness's tomorrow. If we could perhaps adjourn until tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Madam, it's almost 7.00. As I told you a moment ago, we'll have to stop there. You will be taken over by the witness service. They will look after you during the evening, and they will bring you back tomorrow morning. Between now and then, please do not discuss the case with anyone, and we'll have the pleasure of seeing you back here tomorrow. I wish everybody a pleasant evening, and we reconvene at 2.15 tomorrow afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 24th day of August 2006, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 6.56 p.m.,
